About

Researcher. Writer.
Policy Advocate.

Cody Ares Baynori is a Georgetown University graduate student in Government with experience across Congress and the Executive Branch — most recently as a Legislative Analyst at USDA under the Biden-Harris administration and as an aide on the Democratic staff of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

Raised in Northern Kentucky by a single mother after his father's deportation, Cody Ares came of age as a queer, Chicano kid acutely aware of the systems that fail working families. He channeled that awareness into early civic engagement — organizing, campaigning, and earning the Northern Kentucky Pride Youth Activist of the Year Award in 2019.

He holds a B.A. in Political Science and English from Columbia University, where he chaired the Student Governing Board and oversaw $1.5 million in student life funding. He is a Kentucky Governor's Scholar and recipient of the Scholars for the Dream Award (CCCC, 2023) and Columbia's "Principled Action" award.

He lives and works in Washington, D.C.

"I want to give thanks to the other student leaders who have entrusted me to lead during some of our toughest and most challenging times."

— Cody Ares Baynori Columbia College Principled Action Award, 2023

Policy Areas & Record

Areas of Work &
Legislative History

Water Resources & Infrastructure

I grew up in Newport, Kentucky along the Ohio River. Bridges, levees, and river traffic shaped daily life and the local economy. On the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee I helped draft portions of the Water Resources Development Act and worked through the technical process that turns local infrastructure needs into federal law. That work involved coordinating with engineers, agency staff, and committee lawyers to translate project proposals into statutory language and committee materials used during hearings and markups.

Environment & Natural Resources

Protecting the environment and confronting climate change will define the coming decades, yet the institutions responsible for managing these risks often move slower than the problems they face. I worked on environmental oversight issues involving PFAS contamination, hazardous chemical regulation, and federal agency accountability. The work required reading technical records, preparing briefing materials, and understanding how regulatory authority actually operates. Those experiences shaped my interest in how environmental governance works in practice and how public health protections are enforced.

Economic Development

I grew up below the poverty line in Northern Kentucky and attended a career and technical education high school. Many classmates moved directly into the workforce while others tried to piece together a path forward. That experience shaped how I think about regional development and economic mobility. I later worked on policy related to the Economic Development Administration and studied energy transition in Appalachian coal communities. Those experiences grounded my interest in how federal investment reaches places that have long struggled with disinvestment.

Agriculture

Agriculture was never an abstract policy topic to me. I grew up in Kentucky in a household that relied on SNAP and attended schools where free lunches were often sourced from nearby farms. Trips to local farms and conversations with producers made it clear how closely food, land, and community are tied together. Later I worked on federal farm policy and congressional briefings on conservation and agricultural programs. Agriculture touches food security, trade, conservation, and rural economies. Farmers sustain communities and steward land that the country depends on.

Government Budgeting

Federal budgeting determines whether public institutions have the resources to function. I spend much of my time reading appropriations bills, committee reports, and agency budget documents to understand how Congress directs funding and how agencies interpret those decisions. At a time when federal spending is intensely debated, it is striking how often investments in public goods face the earliest pressure. Budget choices shape schools, infrastructure, and local services. Careful attention to how money moves through government reveals which priorities actually receive support.

Workforce & Labor Markets

My interest in workforce policy began long before graduate research. I worked in grocery stores and bars and spent early shifts unloading trucks as a clerk at Kroger in a union shop. Scheduling, pay, and workplace expectations were daily concerns. Today I study labor markets through research using federal employment and census data to understand hiring patterns and credential requirements. Seeing work from both sides gives me a grounded perspective on how economic policy affects the people whose livelihoods depend on it.

Emerging Technology & Artificial Intelligence

New technologies shape employment, education, and economic opportunity across sectors. My academic research examines how artificial intelligence influences hiring patterns, credential expectations, and career outcomes. Earlier work at Columbia involved research on natural language processing systems and questions of bias and inequality in automated decision making. Technology policy requires careful attention to both technical design and social impact. Understanding how emerging tools interact with labor markets and institutions remains central to responsible governance.

Criminal Justice Reform

My work in criminal justice began with reviewing case records involving potential wrongful convictions and post sentencing relief. That experience required careful reading of trial documents, witness statements, and investigative records. I also conducted policy research within an inspector general office focused on oversight of police practices. These settings demanded precision and evidence based analysis. They reinforced how accountability systems operate and how much depends on thorough documentation, careful review, and clear reporting.

Disaster Recovery & Resilience

Disasters test whether institutions can coordinate quickly and deliver resources where they are needed. I worked on federal disaster response issues involving watershed recovery programs, wildfire response, and emergency funding requests. During my time on a Senate committee I was also present during federal coordination efforts following the Baltimore bridge collapse, which required rapid communication between agencies, Congress, and state officials. These experiences showed how disaster policy moves from legislation to operational response under real pressure.

Civic Participation

My involvement in politics began through LGBTQ advocacy in Northern Kentucky. I helped organize and support Gay Straight Alliances in local schools and was recognized as the 2019 NKY Pride Youth Activist of the Year. Those experiences introduced me to civic engagement and the importance of building spaces where people feel comfortable participating in public life. I later worked in congressional offices and other public service roles where constituent concerns arrive daily. Public institutions function best when people believe they belong in them.
